newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Weaker Indonesian rupiah both blight and blessing.
newsitem.headline: Weaker Indonesian rupiah both blight and blessing.

text.p: The sharp decline of the Indonesian rupiah against the U.S. dollar will be both a blessing and blight for the country's corporate sector, officials and analysts said on Thursday.
"There will be some positive effects and there will negative effects," Investment Minister Sanyoto Sastrowardoyo told reporters on the fringes of an international capital market conference.

"It will depend on whether their (companies') market is overseas or local. Whether their loans are from within the country or from overseas," he said after the conference was opened by President Suharto. "It cannot be generalised."
The rupiah plunged to a historic low against the dollar on Thursday after the government decided to scrap its intervention band, effectively floating the currency.
Sanyoto said the decline had yet to impact foreign investment in Indonesia, the world's fourth-most populous country with more than 200 million people.
Central Bank governor Sudradjat Djiwandono told the conference the intervention band was no longer an advantage to Indonesia following similar moves by Thailand and the Philippines.
He said other countries in the region such as Malaysia and Singapore did not have intervention bands.
PT Tambang Timah, the world's largest integrated tin mining company, which is also listed on the London Stock Exchange, is one of the companies expected to benefit from the weak rupiah.
"It will not be a problem," Timah president-director Erry Riana told Reuters. "Our exports are denominated in U.S. dollars."

Erry said the company's second half net profit was expected to be better than its performance in the first six months of this year, when it posted a net profit of 57.30 billion rupiah ($20.8 million) against 70.58 billion rupiah in the year-ago period.
Astra International, Indonesia's largest automobile producer, said it would be hit by the rupiah's decline.
Astra Finance Director Rini Soewandi told a briefing that the company had a loan exposure of $1.6 billion as of end-July denominated in the U.S. currency.
"Astra has a 25 percent open position in July and this means a translation loss of 70 billion rupiah before taxes," she said.
She said, however, that improved performance in the first half of this year has led the company to revise its 1997 net profit forecast to 721 billion rupiah from 627 billion rupiah.
Soewandi said total revenue forecasts for the year had been revised to 16.3 trillion rupiah from 15.4 trillion.
Government-controlled PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (Telkom), the biggest capitalised company on the Jakarta Stock Exchange, said it had total "two-step" loans of about 4.4 trillion rupiah.
Under the two-step loan system, financial institutions lend to the government, which in turn lends to state enterprises.

Telkom chief financial officer Harry Supangkat said only two of the latest two-step loans from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank were in dollars, adding that they were "very small" and already hedged.
Jonathan Zax, corporate development and investor relations director of cigarette-maker PT Hanjaya Mandala Sampoerna, said the company had debts totalling $270 million.
"Our total debt is about $270 million and we are covered on about $225 million of it," he said, adding that the company had hedged at between 2,490-2,520 to the dollar. ($1 = 2,750 rupiah)
